paragraphs: But Kolya did not hear her. At last he could go out. As he went out at the gate he looked around, shrugged his shoulders, and said, “It’s freezing.” Then he went straight along the street and turned right toward the market square. When he reached the last house but one before the square, he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle out of his pocket, and blew it as hard as he could, as if giving a signal. He did not have to wait even a minute. A rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, in a warm, neat, even stylish coat, darted out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin), the son of a well-to-do official. His parents had apparently forbidden him to associate with Krassotkin, who was well known as a hopelessly naughty boy, so Smurov had obviously slipped out on the sly. He was—if the reader has not forgotten—one of the group of boys who two months before had thrown stones at Ilusha. He was the one who had told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
“I’ve been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin,” said Smurov flatly, and the boys set off toward the market square.
“I’m late,” answered Krassotkin. “Circumstances held me up. You won’t get thrashed for coming with me?”
“Come on, I’m never thrashed! And you’ve got Perezvon with you?”
“Yes.”
“You’re taking him too?”
“Yes.”
“Ah! If only it were Zhutchka!”
“That’s impossible. Zhutchka doesn’t exist. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of obscurity.”

“Ah! Couldn’t we do this?” Smurov suddenly stood still. “You see, Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog, like Perezvon. Couldn’t you tell him this is Zhutchka? He might believe you.”
“Boy, shun a lie. That’s one thing. Even with a good aim—that’s another. Above all, I hope you haven’t told them anything about my coming.”

“Heaven forbid! I know what I’m doing. But you won’t comfort him with Perezvon,” said Smurov with a sigh. “You know his father, the captain, ‘the wisp of tow,’ told us he was going to bring him a real mastiff pup today, with a black nose. He thinks that would comfort Ilusha, but I doubt it.”
“And how is Ilusha?”

“Ah, he’s bad, very bad! I think he’s in consumption. He’s quite conscious, but his breathing! His breathing’s gone wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots put on so he could be led around the room. He tried to walk, but he couldn’t stand. ‘Ah, I told you before, father,’ he said, ‘those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.’ He thought it was his boots that made him stagger, but it was really just weakness. He won’t live another week. Herzenstube is looking after him. Now they’re rich again—they’ve got heaps of money.”
“They’re rogues.”
“Who’s a rogue?”

“Doctors, and the whole crew of quacks together, and individually too, of course. I don’t believe in medicine. It’s a useless institution. I mean to look into all that. But what’s this sentimentality you’ve got going up there? The whole class seems to be there every day.”
“Not the whole class. It’s only ten of our fellows who go to see him every day. There’s nothing in that.”

“What I don’t understand in all this is the part Alexey Karamazov is playing. His brother is going to be tried tomorrow or the next day for such a crime, and yet he has so much time to spend on sentimentality with boys.”
“There’s no sentimentality in it. You’re going yourself now to make it up with Ilusha.”
“Make it up with him? What an absurd expression! But I don’t allow anyone to analyze my actions.”
“And how glad Ilusha will be to see you! He has no idea you’re coming. Why was it, why was it you wouldn’t come all this time?” Smurov cried with sudden warmth.

“My dear boy, that’s my business, not yours. I’m going of my own accord because I choose to, but you’ve all been dragged there by Alexey Karamazov—there’s a difference, you know. And how do you know? Maybe I’m not going to make it up at all. It’s a stupid expression.”

“It’s not Karamazov at all. It’s not his doing. Our fellows started going there on their own. Of course, they went with Karamazov at first. And there’s been nothing of that sort—no silliness. First one went, and then another. His father was awfully glad to see us. You know, he’ll simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He can see Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we’ve made it up with Ilusha. Ilusha asked about you, that was all. He just asks and says no more. His father will go out of his mind or hang himself. He behaved like a madman before. You know, he’s a very decent man. We made a mistake then. It’s all the fault of that murderer who beat him then.”

“Karamazov is a riddle to me all the same. I could have made his acquaintance long ago, but in some cases I like to keep a proper pride. Besides, I have a theory about him that I must work out and test.”

Kolya fell into dignified silence. Smurov was silent too. Smurov, of course, worshiped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on a level with him. Now he was tremendously interested that Kolya had said he was “going of himself” to see Ilusha. He felt there must be some mystery in Kolya’s suddenly taking it into his head to go to him that day. They crossed the market square, where at that hour there were many loaded wagons from the country and a great number of live fowls. The market women were selling rolls, cottons, threads and so on in their booths. These Sunday markets were naïvely called “fairs” in the town, and there were many such fairs in the year.
Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing first on one side, then on the other. When he met other dogs, they eagerly sniffed each other over according to the rules of canine etiquette.
“I like to watch such realistic scenes, Smurov,” said Kolya suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff at one another when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”
“Yes. It’s a funny habit.”

“No, it’s not funny. You’re wrong there. There’s nothing funny in nature, however funny it may seem to man with his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they’d be sure to find just as much that was funny in the social relations of men, their masters—if not far more. I say that again, because I’m convinced there’s far more foolishness among us. That’s Rakitin’s idea—a remarkable idea. I’m a Socialist, Smurov.”
“And what’s a Socialist?” asked Smurov.

“That’s when everyone is equal and everyone owns property in common, there are no marriages, and everyone has whatever religion and laws he likes best, and all the rest of it. You’re not old enough to understand that yet. It’s cold, though.”
“Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father looked at the thermometer just now.”

“Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the middle of winter we don’t feel so cold, even with fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost, as we do now, at the beginning of winter, when there’s a sudden frost of twelve degrees, especially when there’s not much snow? It’s because people aren’t used to it. Everything is habit with men, everything, even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great motive power. What a funny-looking peasant!”

Kolya pointed to a tall peasant with a good-natured face, in a long sheepskin coat, who was standing by his wagon, clapping his hands together in their shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was all white with frost.
“That peasant’s beard is frozen,” Kolya cried in a loud, provoking voice as he passed him.
“Lots of people’s beards are frozen,” the peasant replied calmly and sententiously.
“Don’t provoke him,” said Smurov.
“It’s all right. He won’t be cross. He’s a nice fellow. Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by.”
“Is your name Matvey?”
“Yes. Didn’t you know?”
“No, I didn’t. It was a guess.”
“You don’t say! You’re a schoolboy, I suppose?”
“Yes.”
“You get whipped, I expect?”
“Nothing to speak of—sometimes.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Well, yes, it does.”
“Ech, what a life!” The peasant heaved a sigh from the bottom of his heart.
“Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by. You’re a nice chap, that you are.”
The boys went on.
“That was a nice peasant,” Kolya remarked to Smurov. “I like talking to the peasants, and I’m always glad to do them justice.”
“Why did you tell a lie, pretending we’re thrashed?” asked Smurov.
“I had to say it to please him.”
“What do you mean?”

“You know, Smurov, I don’t like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to understand at the first word. Some things can’t be explained. According to a peasant’s notions, schoolboys are whipped, and must be whipped. What would a schoolboy be if he weren’t whipped? And if I told him we aren’t, he’d be disappointed. But you don’t understand that. One has to know how to talk to the peasants.”
“Only don’t tease them, please, or you’ll get into another scrape like the one about that goose.”
“So you’re afraid?”
“Don’t laugh, Kolya. Of course I’m afraid. My father would be awfully angry. I’m strictly forbidden to go out with you.”
“Don’t worry, nothing will happen this time. Hello, Natasha!” he shouted to a market woman in one of the booths.
“Calling me Natasha! What next! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged market woman shouted back at him.
“I’m so glad it’s Marya. Good-by!”
“Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you carrying on like that!”
“I’m in a hurry. I can’t stay now. You can tell me next Sunday.” Kolya waved his hand at her, as though she had attacked him and not he her.
“I’ve nothing to tell you next Sunday. You set upon me, you impudent young monkey. I didn’t say anything,” bawled Marya. “You want a whipping, that’s what you want, you saucy jackanapes!”

There was a roar of laughter among the other market women around her. Suddenly a man in a violent rage darted out from the arcade of shops close by. He was a young man, not a native of the town, with dark, curly hair and a long, pale face marked with smallpox. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap, and looked like a merchant’s clerk. He was in a state of stupid excitement and shook his fist at Kolya.
“I know you!” he cried angrily. “I know you!”
Kolya stared at him. He could not recall when he could have had a row with the man. But he had been in so many rows in the street that he could hardly remember them all.
“Do you?” he asked sarcastically.
“I know you! I know you!” the man repeated idiotically.
“So much the better for you. Well, it’s time I was going. Good-by!”
“You’re at your saucy pranks again?” cried the man. “You’re at your saucy pranks again? I know, you’re at it again!”
“It’s not your business, brother, if I’m at my saucy pranks again,” said Kolya, standing still and looking him over.
“Not my business?”
“No, it’s not your business.”
“Whose then? Whose then? Whose then?”
“It’s Trifon Nikititch’s business, not yours.”
“What Trifon Nikititch?” asked the youth, staring at Kolya with loutish amazement, but still as angry as ever.
Kolya looked him over gravely.
“Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he asked suddenly, with stern emphasis.
“What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven’t,” said the young man, somewhat taken aback.
“Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya went on, even more emphatically and even more severely.
“What Sabaneyev? No, I don’t know him.”

“Well then, you can go to the devil,” said Kolya, cutting the conversation short. He turned sharply to the right and strode quickly on his way, as though he scorned any more talk with a dolt who did not even know Sabaneyev.
“Stop, hey! What Sabaneyev?” the young man recovered from his moment of stupefaction and was as excited as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women with a silly stare.
The women laughed.
“You can never tell what he’s after,” said one of them.
“What Sabaneyev is it he’s talking about?” the young man repeated, still furious and waving his right arm.
“It must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that’s who it must be,” one of the women suggested.
The young man stared at her wildly.
“For the Kuzmitchovs?” repeated another woman. “But his name wasn’t Trifon. His name is Kuzma, not Trifon. But the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can’t be the same man.”

“His name isn’t Trifon and it isn’t Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov,” put in a third woman suddenly, who had been silent until then, listening gravely. “Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”
“No doubt about it, it’s Tchizhov,” a fourth woman confirmed emphatically.
The bewildered youth looked from one to another.
“But what did he ask for, what did he ask for, good people?” he cried, almost in desperation. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ says he. And who the devil is supposed to know who Sabaneyev is?”
“You’re a senseless fellow. I’m telling you it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that’s who it is!” one of the women shouted at him impressively.
“What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”
“That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer.”
“And what has your Tchizhov got to do with me, good people, eh?”

“How can I tell what he’s got to do with you?” put in another. “You ought to know yourself what you want with him, if you make such a clamor about him. He spoke to you, he didn’t speak to us, you fool. Don’t you really know him?”
“Know who?”
“Tchizhov.”
“The devil take Tchizhov, and you with him. I’ll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!”
“Going to give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he’ll give you one. You’re a fool, that’s what you are!”
“Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischievous woman. I’ll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

The woman guffawed. But Kolya was by now a long way off, marching along with a triumphant air. Smurov walked beside him, looking back at the shouting group far behind. He too was in high spirits, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya’s company.
“Which Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, already guessing what the answer would be.

“How should I know? Now there’ll be an uproar among them all day. I like to stir up fools in every class of society. There’s another blockhead, that peasant there. You know, they say ‘there’s no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,’ but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just as much. Can’t you see it all over his face that he’s a fool, that peasant, eh?”
“Leave him alone, Kolya. Let’s go on.”
“Nothing could stop me now that I’m off. Hey, good morning, peasant!”
A sturdy-looking peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard, who was walking by, raised his head and looked at the boy. He seemed not quite sober.
“Good morning, if you’re not laughing at me,” he answered slowly.
“And if I am?” laughed Kolya.
“Well, a joke’s a joke. Laugh away. I don’t mind. There’s no harm in a joke.”
“Sorry, brother, it was a joke.”
“Well, God forgive you!”
“Do you forgive me, too?”
“I forgive you completely. Go along.”
“I say, you seem a clever peasant.”
“Cleverer than you,” the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
“I doubt it,” said Kolya, somewhat taken aback.
“It’s true, though.”
“Perhaps it is.”
“It is, brother.”
“Good-by, peasant!”
“Good-by!”
“There are all sorts of peasants,” Kolya remarked to Smurov after a short silence. “How could I know I’d hit on a clever one? I’m always ready to recognize intelligence in the peasantry.”

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half-past eleven. The boys hurried. They covered the long way to Captain Snegiryov’s lodging quickly and almost in silence. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go on ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
“One must sniff around a bit first,” he said to Smurov.
“Why ask him to come out?” Smurov protested. “You go in. They’ll be awfully glad to see you. What’s the sense of making friends out here in the frost?”
“I know why I want to see him out here in the frost,” Kolya cut him short, in the despotic tone he liked to use with “small boys,” and Smurov ran to do his bidding.
